TimeIndex::searchsorted¶

Back to TimeIndex API Reference

Signature¶

TimeIndex::searchsorted(const Timeline& key, bool right = false) const -> std::int64_t

What It Does¶

Returns the insertion position for a scalar timestamp in the sorted index.

This is the temporal equivalent of a lower-bound or upper-bound search:

  • right = false gives the left insertion point.

  • right = true gives the right insertion point.

That makes searchsorted() a load-bearing primitive for building time slices, bucketing event streams, or mapping ad-hoc timestamps into the nearest valid interval boundary.

At the TimeIndex level, this is one of the most fundamental ordered-axis questions: if this timestamp were inserted here, where would it land?

Parameters¶

key

The timestamp to insert. It must be a scalar Timeline, not a vector of times.

If your input is still text, parse or construct the scalar timestamp first and then search against the axis.

right

Controls which side of equal timestamps is chosen.

  • false Return the first valid insertion position.

  • true Return the insertion position after any equal timestamps already present.

Returns¶

std::int64_t An insertion position in [0, size()].

Examples¶

Example 1. Find the insertion position for an in-between timestamp.

auto idx = pluss::timeindex::make({
    "2024-11-01T00:00:00Z",
    "2024-11-01T00:20:00Z",
    "2024-11-01T00:40:00Z",
    "2024-11-01T01:00:00Z",
    "2024-11-01T01:20:00Z",
});

auto key = pluss::timeline::make("2024-11-01T00:55:00Z");

auto left_pos = idx.searchsorted(key, false);
auto right_pos = idx.searchsorted(key, true);
std::cout << "left_pos = " << left_pos << "\n";
std::cout << "right_pos = " << right_pos << "\n";

Output¶

left_pos = 3
right_pos = 3

Example 2. Toggle right when you care about which side of an equal run should own the insertion point.

auto pos = idx.searchsorted(key, /*right=*/true);
std::cout << "pos = " << pos << "\n";

This distinction becomes important once duplicates exist and you need to decide whether the new case belongs before or after the equal block.

Notes¶

  • searchsorted() expects a scalar key. Passing a vector of keys is not this method’s job.

  • right = false behaves like a left insertion point.

  • right = true behaves like an upper-bound style insertion point.

  • The semantics only make sense against a sorted TimeIndex.

  • Use searchsorted() when you need the raw insertion logic itself. Use slice() or asof() when you want a higher-level answer built on top of the same ordering semantics.

  • This is one of the core building blocks underneath slice, slice_time, and asof-style logic.

See Also¶

  • TimeIndex::asof: get the last observed timestamp position at or before a key.

  • TimeIndex::slice: turn two temporal bounds into a range of matching case positions.
